_what_this_is: EVERY state the two update surfaces can be in, and what each one must say.
One table, both readers: the briefing line (framework/frontdoor/run_briefing,
_update_notice + _update_refusal_line, pytest) and the home card
(cabinet/dashboard/src/lib/updates, updateHeadline + refusalToShow, vitest).
Each reader is driven on the SAME bytes -- `state` is written verbatim as
.updates/state.json, the `receipt_seeds` entry named by a row's `receipt` axis
is emitted into a throwaway ledger through the REAL emitter, and the card's
status object is `resolved` plus these fields
exactly as `cabinet-update.sh status --json` derives its report.
WHY AN EXHAUSTIVE TABLE AND NOT MORE ARMS. Four review rounds each found one
more adjacent state in these same two readers: a refusal that outlived the
bundle it was about (round 1), a refusal that spoke over a running apply
(round 2), a refusal that outlived the apply that overtook it (round 3), and a
whole SECOND refusal channel that none of the rules had ever been applied to
(round 4). Every arm written for each of them was aimed at the state that
already worked. Hand-written arms cannot close that class, because the defect
is always in the state nobody thought to write an arm for. A product does not
have to be thought of.
WHY THERE ARE SIX AXES AND NOT FIVE. Round 4's defect lived exactly where the
240-row table did not look: all 240 rows ran on an EMPTY LEDGER, and the
briefing had a second refusal channel -- the ledger receipt -- that spoke
outside the four rules and that the card could not see at all. A completeness
claim that holds one input constant is a green hole, not a covered one. The
ledger is now an axis.
THE AXES (5 x 3 x 4 x 2 x 2 x 6 = 1440 rows, the whole product, nothing skipped):
phase          idle | refused | applying | applied | rolled_back
waiting        none | same (the bundle the refusal is about) | other
refusal        none | locked-paths | busy | digest-mismatch   (in state.json)
ledger_error   absent | set (A5.16: the ledger FAILED, not a version behind)
event_fallback false | true (a record held for a ledger one version behind)
receipt        none | refused-same-sha | refused-other-sha | refused-busy |
applied | rolled_back                          (in the ledger)
`waiting` folds presence and sha identity into one 3-valued axis; a refusal is
always ABOUT the `refused` sha, so `same`/`other` is what scopes it. The
`receipt` axis carries ONE receipt about the `refused` sha, except
`refused-other-sha`, which is about the `landed` sha -- one row of each shape
is enough because the resolver reduces the ledger to at most one current
refusal, and which bundle it is about is what every rule then turns on.
WHICH RECEIPT ROWS ARE REACHABLE, and why the unreachable ones stay. Reachable
today: every combination where the state file and the ledger AGREE (both
written by one `record_refusal` call, in that order), and every combination
where the ledger has a record the state file does not -- a failed or truncated
state write, a removed file, an install carrying refusals recorded before this
branch. Not reachable from any writer: a state file carrying refusal X while
the ledger's current refusal is about a different bundle Y. They are KEPT and
pinned for the same reason the degenerate `phase` rows are: a state file can be
truncated or hand-edited, a ledger can be restored from a copy, and what a
reader does at the degenerate end is exactly what four rounds of arms never
asked. Nothing here is skipped.
THE RULES, from the contract (A5.13, A5.15, A5.16) and not from either
implementation.
RESOLUTION FIRST, and it is ONE record. A refusal is written down twice by one
call and either half can be the only one that survives, so both surfaces read
one resolved `last_refusal`: the state file's record if it has one (either
`last_refusal` or the top-level copy a `refused` document carries), else the
ledger's CURRENT refusal, else none. `resolved.source` says which channel
answered. Currency on the receipt channel is the receipt spelling of `phase:
refused`: the newest `cabinet_update_refused` receipt speaks only while nothing
has happened to that bundle since. `resolved.last_refusal.ts` is null on a
receipt-sourced record because the ledger stamps it -- no reader branches on
`ts`.
THEN THE FOUR RULES, applied once, to that one record. `refusal_speaks` is the
sub-surface -- refusalToShow non-null on the card, a non-empty
_update_refusal_line on the briefing -- and it is the same on BOTH surfaces on
every row, because it is one property of one record:
1. No refusal on record: it never speaks.
2. An apply IN FLIGHT outranks it. `applying` is the live state; a refusal
recorded before the retry that is running now is a note about a request.
3. Nothing waiting: it speaks only while it is still the LAST THING THAT
HAPPENED, i.e. phase `refused`. An apply or a rollback since has
overtaken it, and `last_refusal` is carried through every write for ever,
so without this rule one refusal silences the applied and rolled-back
sentences on both surfaces for the life of the install.
4. Something waiting: it speaks only if it is a verdict ON THOSE BYTES --
the same sha, and a reason about the bundle rather than about timing
(`busy` means another updater held the lock).
THE HEADLINE KINDS: ready | refused | applying | applied | rolled_back |
fault | quiet. The two surfaces rank them the same except for two deliberate
differences of SHAPE, both written per surface here rather than skipped:
(a) THE LEDGER FAULT. The briefing has ONE line and spends it on a ledger
fault above everything but a refusal (A5.16 -- a full disk announced as a
version number is a fault nobody goes back to look at), while the card
has room to show the fault as a sub-line beside whatever its headline
says.
(b) A ROLLED-BACK RECEIPT ABOUT THE WAITING BUNDLE. The briefing spends its
one line saying that the bundle in the inbox is one this box already
tried and put back; the card says `Update ready` and keeps Apply. These
do not contradict each other -- a rollback is not a refusal, and
retrying one is a reasonable thing to do, exactly as the card keeps
Apply for a digest mismatch. What must never differ is `refusal_speaks`,
which is what withdraws Apply, and it does not.
The wording differs everywhere, which is why what is asserted is the kind.
A FAULT IS NEVER HEADLINE-LESS. The card renders at all only when its
headline is non-null, so `fault` is the card's LAST arm: it takes the
headline only where nothing else has one, which is the only way `named on
every surface` can be true of a surface that can decline to appear.
A kind flipped here reds BOTH suites. A row whose code disagrees with this
table is a defect in the code -- this table is derived from the contract, and
the code is what has been wrong four times.
